docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis
docs.text:
Quantitative analysis tools for sidescan data.

Each function takes data and returns a result dataclass (with to_dict()); none runs a workflow or plots (see :mod:sidescanpy.viz.analysis and :mod:sidescanpy.viz.tvg).

  • :func:characterize_values / :func:infer_units — value-range summary and units call (:class:ValueSummary, :class:UnitsResult).
  • :func:compare_outlier_rejection — effect of range-binned outlier rejection (:class:OutlierComparisonResult).
  • :func:analyze_nadir — nadir type, altitude and first-bottom-return boundaries (:class:NadirResult).
  • :func:estimate_beam_geometry — near/far beam edges (:class:BeamGeometryResult).
  • :func:estimate_usable_range — where signal falls to the noise floor (:class:UsableRangeResult).
  • :func:fit_range_decay — TVG-status classification from a range-decay fit (:class:RangeDecayResult); :func:fit_tvg_curve, :func:compare_before_after, :func:bin_by_altitude are its building blocks.
  • :func:summarize_navigation — heading convention and nav/attitude stats (:class:NavigationSummary).
  • :func:measure_ping_geometry — ping spacing and resolution (:class:PingGeometry).
  • :func:detect_shadow_proposals — object proposals from acoustic shadows and their highlights (:class:ShadowProposals).

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.beam
docs.text:
Beam geometry from measured boundaries.

:func:estimate_beam_geometry triangulates the sidescan beam's near and far edges from data already measured elsewhere:

  • near edge, per (ping, channel): arccos(altitude / slant_range) at the first bottom return (:func:~sidescanpy.analysis.nadir.analyze_nadir);
  • far edge, survey-wide: arctan(usable_range / altitude) with the usable range from :func:~sidescanpy.analysis.usable_range.estimate_usable_range.

A wrong altitude_m shifts both edges together, so this can't by itself separate a tilted beam from bad altitude.

docs.title: BeamGeometryResult dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

Near/far beam-edge angles (degrees from vertical).

confidence reflects the cross-ping near-edge measurement: "determined", "ambiguous" (too much ping-to-ping spread), "undetermined" (too few valid pings), or None when the reference ping's altitude is unusable. near_ray / far_ray hold the single ping_idx geometry per side ("port", "starboard") for plotting. Far-edge values are None without a usable range.

docs.text:
infer_units(
    summary: ValueSummary,
    decay: RangeDecayResult | None = None,
) -> UnitsResult

Classify likely units from a value-range signature.

  • mostly negative, within (-200, 5] → "dB"
  • non-negative, max in (0, 1] → "normalized"
  • non-negative, max > 1 → "raw_counts" (raw ADC counts or uncalibrated linear amplitude; volts can't be told apart by value alone)
  • anything else → "unknown"

When decay (a :func:~sidescanpy.analysis.tvg.fit_range_decay result) has a confident TVG status and a fixed-scale RMSE under 3 dB, a supporting note is added.

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.geometry
docs.text:
Ping geometry measurements for one section of a survey.

:func:measure_ping_geometry measures median along-track ping spacing, across-track swath width and range-axis sample interval — the native resolutions to choose an export pixel size from.

docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

Native sampling of a section, in metres; None where not measurable.

docs.title: measure_ping_geometry
docs.text:
measure_ping_geometry(
    ds: Dataset,
    *,
    low_pct: float = 1.0,
    high_pct: float = 99.0,
) -> PingGeometry

Median ping spacing, swath width and sample interval of ds.

  • ping_spacing_m_median: median nonzero along-track step between consecutive pings (needs at least 2 pings).
  • swath_width_m: high_pct minus low_pct percentile of across_track_m (robust to a few far-flung samples).
  • sample_interval_m: median per-ping step of slant_range_m on channel 0.

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.nadir
docs.text:
Nadir analysis: how nadir is represented, and where the bottom starts.

:func:analyze_nadir classifies the first nadir_n_samples of each ping (gap / bright_spike / noisy / clean) and reports two distinct reference points per (ping, channel):

  • the altitude sample — the vehicle altitude in sample units (where ground_range_m first goes finite). Not a boundary of the data.
  • the first bottom return — where backscatter actually rises to the bottom echo (:func:~sidescanpy.processing.bottom.detect_first_bottom_return), floored at the altitude sample. Everything before it is the nadir gap: blanking, noise, and the span the tilted beam never illuminates.

Built on :mod:sidescanpy.processing.bottom.

docs.title: NadirResult dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

Nadir classification and bottom-boundary statistics.

nadir_type is "gap", "bright_spike", "noisy" or "clean". Sample-index statistics are None when not computed. The per-(ping, channel) arrays altitude_sample and first_bottom_return_sample are left out of to_dict().

docs.title: analyze_nadir
docs.text:
analyze_nadir(
    ds: Dataset,
    value_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    range_var: str = "ground_range_m",
    *,
    nadir_n_samples: int = 50,
    bright_spike_ratio: float = 1.5,
    noisy_std_ratio: float = 1.5,
    gap_pct_zero_threshold: float = 20.0,
    water_column_post_window: int = 20,
    strong_return_smooth_window: int = 10,
    strong_return_threshold_fraction: float = 0.2,
    strong_return_min_run: int = 10,
    strong_return_min_sample_buffer: float = 0.0,
    strong_return_peak_percentile: float = 100.0,
    min_first_bottom_return_sample: float | None = None,
    boundary_smoothing_window: int = 15,
) -> NadirResult

Classify nadir and locate the altitude sample and first bottom return.

Classification (first match wins), comparing samples [0, nadir_n_samples) against the rest of each ping:

  • gap — at least gap_pct_zero_threshold % of nadir values are 0
  • bright_spike — nadir/off-nadir mean ratio >= bright_spike_ratio
  • noisy — nadir/off-nadir std ratio >= noisy_std_ratio
  • clean — otherwise

A corroborating step check compares the mean of water_column_post_window samples on either side of the first bottom return on the middle ping (channel 0) and adds a note if the signal doesn't step up.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default range_var str

Used for the altitude sample. If absent, that part is skipped with a note; the first bottom return is still detected (without the altitude floor).

"ground_range_m" strong_return_smooth_window int 10 strong_return_threshold_fraction int 10 strong_return_min_run int 10 strong_return_min_sample_buffer int 10 strong_return_peak_percentile float

Passed to :func:~sidescanpy.processing.bottom.detect_first_bottom_return as smooth_window / threshold_fraction / min_run / min_sample_buffer / peak_percentile.

100.0 min_first_bottom_return_sample float

Extra scalar floor on the first bottom return, combined with the altitude floor by element-wise max.

None boundary_smoothing_window int

:func:~sidescanpy.processing.bottom.smooth_boundary_across_pings window for the first bottom return; <= 1 disables.

15

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.navigation
docs.text:
Navigation and attitude data-quality summary.

:func:summarize_navigation reports per-field statistics for the per-ping aux fields (heading, pitch, roll, altitude, depth, heave) and checks which heading convention the data follows. The library's own convention is compass bearing, clockwise from north, in [0, 360).

docs.title: FieldStats dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

NaN count and finite min/max/mean of one per-ping field.

docs.title: NavigationSummary dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

Per-field statistics plus the heading-convention check.

heading_convention is "compass_bearing" (all finite values in [0, 360)), "signed" (all in [-180, 180)), "ambiguous" (neither holds for every value), or None (no heading, or no finite heading values). field_stats is keyed by variable name and covers the NAV_ATTITUDE_VARS present.

docs.title: summarize_navigation
docs.text:
summarize_navigation(
    ds: Dataset, *, heading_var: str = "heading_deg"
) -> NavigationSummary

Per-field statistics for every NAV_ATTITUDE_VARS entry in ds, plus the fraction of heading_var values in each heading convention.

A value outside both conventions is not necessarily an error (a trace through a turn can briefly leave one), so the plotted trace is the place to judge it.

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.shadows
docs.text:
Object proposals from acoustic shadows in native slant-range data.

An object standing proud of the seabed returns a highlight on its near-range face and leaves a shadow (little or no return) behind it, further out along the same pings. :func:detect_shadow_proposals finds those shadows as regions well below the local seabed level, pairs each with the highlight just in front of it, and returns one proposal box per object in native (ping, sample, channel) coordinates, with features (sizes, contrast, an estimated height) to rank or filter them.

The data are averaged into cells about cell_m across track (one ping along track) before thresholding, because single samples carry several dB of speckle. A second, weaker threshold catches the short, shallow shadows of objects close to nadir, where the grazing angle is steep; those regions are kept only with a highlight in front of them. Proposals are meant to pre-fill boxes for a person to correct, so the defaults favour recall over precision.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: ShadowProposals dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

Proposals found by :func:detect_shadow_proposals.

proposals has one row per proposal (columns :data:PROPOSAL_COLUMNS). Extents are half-open native positions along the dataset's ping and sample axes, like :class:~sidescanpy.export.windows.native.NativeWindow; the box spans the highlight (when found) and the shadow. height_m is NaN where altitude is unknown. weak marks proposals from the weak-shadow pass. score is in [0, 1]: higher for a deeper shadow, a taller object (a longer shadow where altitude is unknown) and a highlight in front.

docs.title: detect_shadow_proposals
docs.text:
detect_shadow_proposals(
    ds: Dataset,
    *,
    value_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    channels: tuple[int, ...] = (0, 1),
    cell_m: float = 0.06,
    background_m: tuple[float, float] = (3.0, 6.0),
    smooth_cells: tuple[int, int] = (1, 3),
    shadow_db: float = 6.0,
    highlight_db: float = 3.0,
    min_shadow_m: float = 0.2,
    min_pings: int = 2,
    max_gap_m: float = 0.6,
    highlight_search_m: float = 2.0,
    min_height_m: float = 0.0,
    max_height_m: float = 3.0,
    max_length_m: float = 8.0,
    weak_shadow_db: float | None = 4.0,
    weak_min_shadow_m: float = 0.1,
    weak_min_highlight: float = 0.5,
    score_height_m: float = 0.3,
    m_per_ping: float | None = None,
) -> ShadowProposals

Find objects by their acoustic shadow.

For each channel:

  1. Average value_var (dB, after the tvg step) into cells of about cell_m along range, one ping each, then smooth them with a smooth_cells (pings, cells) running mean.
  2. Background: a running median over background_m (across, along track, metres).
  3. Shadow cells are at least shadow_db below the background; they are grouped into connected regions (8-connected).
  4. A region is kept if it covers at least min_pings pings and its longest run along range is at least min_shadow_m.
  5. Its highlight is the run of cells at least highlight_db above the background ending within max_gap_m before the shadow, searched up to highlight_search_m towards nadir, on each of its pings.
  6. Height from flat-seabed geometry, h = A * Ls / (R + Ls) (altitude A, slant range R to the shadow start, shadow slant length Ls), per ping, median over the region. Proposals outside [min_height_m, max_height_m] (when the height is known) or longer than max_length_m in either direction are dropped.
  7. Weak pass (unless weak_shadow_db is None): regions at least weak_shadow_db below the background that contain no cell of a proposal from steps 3-6, with a run of at least weak_min_shadow_m, go through steps 4-6 and are kept when a highlight is found on at least weak_min_highlight of their pings. They get weak=True.

score = 0.4 x shadow depth (shadow_db -> 0, 3 * shadow_db -> 1) + 0.3 x height / score_height_m (capped at 1; shadow length / 1 m where the height is unknown) + 0.3 x the fraction of pings with a highlight. Height rather than shadow length, because the shadow of the same object is much shorter near nadir.

NaN cells (blanked water column, hull echo, masked pings) are never shadow, and a region whose near-range side lies within 0.3 m of NaN cells on most of its pings is dropped: that is the edge of the blanked area, not an object.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ds Dataset

One frequency channel (slice pings beforehand to limit memory).

required value_var str

Values in dB.

"backscatter_intensity" channels tuple of int (0, 1) cell_m float

Across-track cell size; rounded to a whole number of samples.

0.06 background_m (float, float)

Background window, across track and along track (m).

(3.0, 6.0) smooth_cells (int, int)

Running-mean size (pings, cells) applied before thresholding.

(1, 3) shadow_db float

Thresholds below / above the background (dB).

6.0, 3.0 highlight_db float

Thresholds below / above the background (dB).

6.0, 3.0 min_shadow_m float 0.2 min_pings int 2 max_gap_m float 0.6 highlight_search_m float 2.0 min_height_m float 0.0, 3.0 max_height_m float 0.0, 3.0 max_length_m float 8.0 weak_shadow_db float or None

Threshold of the weak pass (dB below background); None skips it.

4.0 weak_min_shadow_m float 0.1 weak_min_highlight float

Fraction of a weak region's pings that must have a highlight.

0.5 score_height_m float

Height that earns the full height part of the score.

0.3 m_per_ping float

Along-track spacing; default from the per-ping positions.

None

Returns:

Type Description ShadowProposals

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.tvg
docs.text:
TVG analysis: backscatter-vs-range profiles and hardware-TVG detection.

Profiles and comparisons:

  • :func:backscatter_vs_range, :func:backscatter_vs_sample — binned statistics (re-exported from :mod:sidescanpy.processing.profiles).
  • :func:compare_before_after — raw vs. TVG-corrected dB and the applied gain, side by side.
  • :func:bin_by_altitude — split pings into equal-count altitude bins.

Detecting what TVG the data already carries:

  • :func:fit_tvg_curve — fit four single-term candidate loss models (flat, spreading_only, absorption_only, full_physics) to an observed loss-vs-range curve (:class:TVGCandidateFitResult).
  • :func:fit_range_decay — bin a dataset, fit the candidates and classify which terms hardware has already removed (:class:RangeDecayResult).

docs.title: TVGCandidateFit dataclass
docs.text:
One candidate loss model fit against an observed loss-vs-range curve.

scale is the least-squares multiplier on the candidate's model (near 1: the data decays like that model as written; near 0: that term is essentially absent) and rmse_db its residual. fixed_scale_rmse_db is the residual with the scale pinned to 1 — the literal physics model. Candidates are ranked by the fixed-scale value, because a free scale on one term can absorb unrelated range-dependent effects and win on RMSE alone. For flat (model identically zero) both values are equal.

docs.title: TVGCandidateFitResult dataclass
docs.text: All four candidate fits for one curve, plus the best by fixed-scale RMSE.

docs.title: RangeDecayResult dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

TVG-status classification from a range-decay fit.

tvg_status names what hardware has already removed: "none", "spreading_only", "absorption_only", "full", or "ambiguous" (winner not clearly ahead, or too little data). best_rmse_db is the winner's fixed-scale RMSE (the ranking criterion); best_free_fit_* are its free-scale values. r_ref_m_override / r_fit_min_m_override record what was requested (e.g. "auto"); r_ref_m / r_fit_min_m what was used. fit (the full :class:TVGCandidateFitResult) is left out of to_dict(); candidates summarizes it.

docs.title: fit_tvg_curve
docs.text:
fit_tvg_curve(
    binned: DataFrame,
    *,
    spreading_loss_db: float = DEFAULT_SPREADING_LOSS_DB,
    absorption_db_per_m: float,
    r_ref_m: float | None = None,
    r_fit_min_m: float | None = None,
    r_fit_max_m: float | None = None,
    min_count_for_r_ref: int = 30,
    fit_fraction: float = 0.6,
    r_ref_search_fraction: float = 0.5,
    value_col: str = "mean",
) -> TVGCandidateFitResult

Fit four candidate hardware-TVG models to a binned raw dB-vs-range curve.

Each candidate is a term (or both) of :func:~sidescanpy.processing.radiometric.tvg_gain_db still present in the data:

  • flat — neither term (hardware compensated both)
  • spreading_only — only spreading_loss_db * log10(R)
  • absorption_only — only 2 * absorption_db_per_m * R
  • full_physics — both (no hardware compensation)

The fitted quantity is observed_loss(r) = value[r_ref] - value[r] (absolute level is unknown). Each candidate gets one free scale, fitted independently: a joint two-term regression is poorly conditioned because the terms are nearly collinear over realistic range spans.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default binned DataFrame

:func:backscatter_vs_range output computed on uncorrected dB backscatter.

required spreading_loss_db float

Spreading coefficient of the spreading_only and full_physics candidates (:data:~sidescanpy.processing.radiometric.DEFAULT_SPREADING_LOSS_DB).

30.0 absorption_db_per_m float

Required; pass the survey's own frequency-appropriate value.

required r_ref_m float

Reference range. Default: the bin with the highest value among bins with count >= min_count_for_r_ref in the near r_ref_search_fraction of the range span (falls back to all eligible bins). Not simply the nearest bin, which often reads low from ring-down/blanking; not the global max, which on flat data can land on a far-range noise bump.

None r_fit_min_m float

Near edge of the fit window. Default r_ref_m (one-sided). Set it lower to fit both sides of the reference.

None r_fit_max_m float

Far edge of the fit window. Default r_ref_m + fit_fraction * (max_range - r_ref_m).

None min_count_for_r_ref int 30 fit_fraction float 0.6 r_ref_search_fraction float 0.5 value_col (mean, median)

Per-bin statistic to fit.

"mean"

Returns:

Type Description TVGCandidateFitResult

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If binned is empty, or no bin has count >= min_count_for_r_ref.

fit_range_decay(
    ds: Dataset,
    value_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    range_var: str = "slant_range_m",
    *,
    already_db: bool = False,
    db_reference_percentile: float = 99.0,
    db_reference_value: float | None = None,
    freq_hz: float | None = None,
    bin_width_m: float = 5.0,
    usable_range_m: float | None = None,
    min_bins: int = 6,
    ambiguous_rel_tol: float = 0.2,
    min_total_count: int = 30,
    exclude_before_sample: ndarray | None = None,
    exclude_first_n_bins: int = 0,
    reject_outliers: bool = False,
    outlier_mad_k: float = 3.5,
    outlier_min_bin_count: int = 5,
    fit_value_col: str = "mean",
    r_ref_m: float | str | None = None,
    r_fit_min_m: float | str | None = None,
    r_fit_min_auto_margin_m: float = _AUTO_NEAR_EDGE_MARGIN_M,
    r_ref_search_fraction: float = 0.5,
    r_ref_window_fraction: float = 1.0 / 3.0,
    channel: int | str | None = None,
    spreading_loss_db: float = DEFAULT_SPREADING_LOSS_DB,
) -> RangeDecayResult

Classify which TVG terms value_var already carries.

Converts to dB, bins by range_var, fits the four :func:fit_tvg_curve candidates and maps the winner (lowest fixed-scale RMSE) to a TVG status. If the runner-up's RMSE is within ambiguous_rel_tol (relative) of the winner's, the status is "ambiguous".

Water-column samples are always excluded via ground_range_m's NaN pattern (when present), independent of range_var.

dB reference

Without calibration an absolute dB level is arbitrary, so linear values are converted relative to the data's own db_reference_percentile (or db_reference_value). Every fit quantity is a dB difference, so this choice does not change the classification.

Name Type Description Default range_var str

Range axis; slant range matches apply_tvg's gain model.

"slant_range_m" already_db bool

value_var is already dB; skip the conversion.

False db_reference_percentile float 99.0 db_reference_value float

Exact linear reference instead of the percentile (e.g. 1.0 for "dB re 1").

None freq_hz float

Default: the channel's center frequency (:func:~sidescanpy.processing.radiometric.center_frequency_hz); sets the absorption term.

None bin_width_m float

Requested bin width; shrunk (never widened) so that usable_range_m spans at least min_bins bins.

5.0 usable_range_m float

Far edge of the fit window.

None min_bins int 6 min_total_count int

Fewer binned samples than this → "ambiguous" without a fit.

30 exclude_before_sample ndarray

(ping, channel) sample index; samples before it are dropped (in dB space) before binning. For aggregate fits pass a uniform boundary (:func:~sidescanpy.processing.bottom.uniform_exclusion_boundary): a per-ping one biases the near-range bins and the reference pick.

None exclude_first_n_bins int

Drop this many nearest bins after binning, before the reference pick and fit — for a bright leading-edge artifact at the bottom return.

0 reject_outliers bool

Run :func:~sidescanpy.processing.outliers.reject_range_outliers on the dB values first (outlier_mad_k, outlier_min_bin_count).

False fit_value_col (mean, median)

Passed to :func:fit_tvg_curve as value_col.

"mean" r_ref_m (float, auto, mid_swath or None)

Reference range. None: :func:fit_tvg_curve's near-field auto-pick. "auto" (recommended with r_fit_min_m="auto"): placed r_ref_window_fraction of the way from the resolved fit window's near edge to usable_range_m, so it always lies inside the window. "mid_swath" (legacy): usable_range_m / 2. Both string modes fall back to the auto-pick, with a note, when usable_range_m is unavailable.

None r_fit_min_m (float, auto or None)

Near edge of the fit window (resolved before r_ref_m). None: one-sided from r_ref_m. "auto": the raw near-field peak bin's far edge plus r_fit_min_auto_margin_m, searched up to a numeric r_ref_m or r_ref_search_fraction * usable_range_m; falls back to None with a note when it can't be resolved. If it ends up beyond a numeric/"mid_swath" r_ref_m it is clamped to it.

docs.title: sidescanpy.analysis.usable_range
docs.text:
Usable range: where the signal falls into the far-range noise floor.

:func:estimate_usable_range bins backscatter by range, estimates the noise floor from the farthest bins, and reports the last range bin whose SNR against that floor still meets a threshold.

docs.title: UsableRangeResult dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ResultMixin

Usable-range estimate and the binned profile it came from.

usable_range_m is None when SNR never meets the threshold or nothing could be binned. binned is the :func:~sidescanpy.processing.profiles.backscatter_vs_range table and snr the per-bin SNR (both serialized as column lists).

docs.title: estimate_usable_range
docs.text:
estimate_usable_range(
    ds: Dataset,
    value_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    range_var: str = "slant_range_m",
    *,
    bin_width_m: float = 2.0,
    snr_threshold: float = 3.0,
    noise_region_fraction: float = 0.1,
    exclude_before_sample: ndarray | None = None,
    reject_outliers: bool = False,
    outlier_mad_k: float = 3.5,
    outlier_min_bin_count: int = 5,
    channel: int | str | None = None,
) -> UsableRangeResult

Estimate the usable range of value_var along range_var.

The noise floor is the median of the per-bin medians over the farthest noise_region_fraction of bins; noise std is the mean of their stds (falling back to the median nonzero bin std). SNR is |bin median - floor| / noise std; the usable range is the far edge of the last bin with SNR >= snr_threshold.

Water-column samples are always excluded using ground_range_m's NaN pattern (when present), independent of range_var.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default range_var str

Range axis to bin by (slant range matches the TVG model's axis).

"slant_range_m" exclude_before_sample ndarray

(ping, channel) sample index; samples before it are dropped before binning, e.g. a per-ping first-bottom-return boundary.

None reject_outliers bool

Run :func:~sidescanpy.processing.outliers.reject_range_outliers first (with outlier_mad_k / outlier_min_bin_count), so the floor reflects a flat-bottom-like population.

False channel int or str

Restrict to one physical side (index, or channel_id value such as "port"). None pools both sides. Applied by masking.

None

docs.title: sidescanpy.core
docs.text:
Core schema, validation, and survey container types.

This module defines the contract that every dataset in SideScanPy must satisfy and provides the top-level objects that user code interacts with.

Public types
  • :class:SideScanFrequencyChannel — single-frequency wrapper around a validated xr.Dataset.
  • :class:SideScanSurvey — multi-frequency container with optional navigation, attitude, DVL, and sensor auxiliary records.
  • :class:Target — format-agnostic sonar contact (see :mod:sidescanpy.core.target).

Validation is provided through xarray accessors:

  • ds.sidescan — validates a single-frequency sonar dataset.
  • ds.navigation_record, ds.attitude_record, ds.dvl_record, ds.sensor_record — validate the corresponding aux stream datasets.
Conventions
  • All time coordinates are datetime64[ns].
  • The channel dimension is always size 2 (port + starboard).
  • ds.attrs["processing_history"] is a JSON-encoded list of step records (see :mod:sidescanpy.core.history); the processing level is derived from it by :func:processing_level.
  • Empty-but-valid aux records (zero observations) are first-class — they validate cleanly and report is_empty() == True.

See docs/core.md for full reference.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: sidescanpy.core.history
docs.text:
Processing history: the record of which correction steps were applied.

ds.attrs["processing_history"] is a JSON-encoded list of step records, appended to by every step that changes a frequency channel dataset::

{
    "step": "tvg",                      # canonical step name
    "params": {...},                    # actual params used, defaults included
    "function": "sidescanpy.processing.radiometric.apply_tvg",
    "version": "0.5.0",                 # sidescanpy version that applied it
    "timestamp_utc": "2026-10-07T12:00:00+00:00",
}

The history is what makes corrections idempotent (a recorded step is not re-applied) and reversible (radiometric steps are undone from their recorded params). The processing level is derived from it (:func:processing_level), not stored as a separate attribute. The history records what the library did; it does not describe the input data (units, hardware TVG state) -- that is the caller's knowledge.

Geometric and georef steps only add variables, so for them a present, not-all-NaN output variable is what counts as "done" (:func:has_step).

Legacy files: step names written by older versions (tvg_correction, compute_geometric_ranges, ...) are mapped to the canonical names by :func:canonical_step, and a legacy processing_level attribute is used only as a fallback when the history records no recognised step.

docs.title: sidescanpy.core.units

Single source for linear <-> dB conversion and the floor-clip artifact.

Convention: every conversion in sidescanpy is amplitude (20log10), because raw backscatter_intensity is linear amplitude. There is no power (10log10) conversion anywhere in the library.

Linear values below :data:MIN_LINEAR are clipped before the log so exact zeros (blanking / ring-down) map to :data:FLOOR_DB instead of -inf. That deterministic floor is an artifact, not a real return; :func:mask_floor_clip / :func:mask_floor_db turn it into NaN.

docs.title: sidescanpy.export
docs.text:
Dataset-export primitives for SideScan sonar surveys.

Distinct from processing/ (physical corrections: TVG, geometric ranges, georeferencing) and export/ml/ (ML annotation file formats): this package turns an already-corrected survey channel into 8-bit training-dataset images — chips or full-channel views, optionally reprojected into geometric or georeferenced meters — plus the shared invertible display transform they're rendered through.

Public entry points
  • :func:to_uint8 / :func:to_uint16 / :func:from_uint8 — invertible percentile+gamma display transform, with a configurable per-image / precomputed (survey- or dataset-wide) normalization scope.
  • :func:compute_reference_stats — precompute percentile bounds shared across many :func:to_uint8 calls, for survey-/dataset-wide scope.
  • :mod:sidescanpy.export.windows — where an image is cut and what is in it: :func:extract_chip / :func:extract_full_channel (plain arrays), :func:extract_pixel_style_window / :func:extract_geo_style_window (one export style at one render level), neighborhood loading, and :func:sample_background_windows (screened no-target windows).
  • :mod:sidescanpy.export.orientation — display orientation of exported windows and their targets.
  • :mod:sidescanpy.export.augment — random flips and jitter.
  • :mod:sidescanpy.export.ml — COCO/YOLO annotation writers.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.augment

Every function takes an explicit numpy.random.Generator so a seeded export is reproducible, and every flip moves the annotated target positions (Target.sample = column, extra_attributes["window_row"] = row) together with the pixels.

docs.text:
Geometric (along-track x across-track meters) windowed export.

Resamples a bounded region directly at an explicit (resolution_m, size_px), centered on a given real-world point — a survey-local frame (no CRS/UTM projection, unlike export.georef_window), using the per-sample across_track_m that processing/geometric.py::compute_geometric_ranges already attaches, and the per-ping cumulative along-track distance from processing.navigation.along_track_distance_m.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: extract_geometric_window
docs.text:
extract_geometric_window(
    channel_ds: Dataset,
    size_px: int,
    *,
    resolution_m: float,
    center_along_m: float,
    center_across_m: float,
    channel_idx: int | None = 0,
    backscatter_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    search_radius_m: float | None = None,
    along_search_radius_m: float | None = None,
    across_search_radius_m: float | None = None,
    avoid_edge_gaps: bool = False,
    along_resolution_m: float | None = None,
    across_resolution_m: float | None = None,
    along_size_px: int | None = None,
    across_size_px: int | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, dict]

Resample a size_px x size_px square region, centered on (center_along_m, center_across_m), at exactly resolution_m meters/pixel on both axes.

Both axes always share the same resolution_m and size_px by construction — no derived-from-extent resolution, no separate resize step, so the result is never stretched relative to the real world (a previous version computed resolution_m from the larger of the window's own along/across extents but still forced both axes to size_px samples — the smaller-extent axis came out visibly stretched; fixed by making resolution and size the only inputs, extent purely a consequence of them). This is still the default — along_resolution_m/across_resolution_m/along_size_px/ across_size_px below are opt-in, and every existing caller that doesn't pass them gets byte-identical square-pixel output.

channel_idx=None pools samples from both channels into the same point cloud instead of one side only — unlike the raw-pixel export.windows primitives, this needs no explicit mirroring: across_track_m is already a real-world coordinate (port negative, starboard positive), so both sides combine correctly by construction, giving a single image spanning the full swath width with the nadir gap naturally in the middle (wherever across_track_m is NaN/near zero on both sides).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default channel_ds Dataset

Already ping-sliced to a neighborhood comfortably containing the requested size_px * resolution_m extent around the center — this function does not itself bound how much source data it searches; a much wider slice than needed just costs more KDTree build time for no benefit.

required size_px int

Output side length in pixels.

required resolution_m float

Meters per pixel, both axes. Pick small (near the channel's own sample interval) for a maximum-detail close-up; pick real_swath_width_m / size_px to fit an entire swath width (both channels) into the frame.

required center_along_m float

Real-world center of the requested window, in the same along-track-distance / across_track_m units the survey's own per-sample geometry uses (e.g. a target's own position, read directly from across_track_m at its ping/sample/channel).

required center_across_m float

Real-world center of the requested window, in the same along-track-distance / across_track_m units the survey's own per-sample geometry uses (e.g. a target's own position, read directly from across_track_m at its ping/sample/channel).

required channel_idx int or None

Restrict to one physical channel (0=port, 1=starboard), or None to pool both.

0 search_radius_m float

Isotropic KDTree query radius (same in both directions); defaults to 1.5 * resolution_m. A survey whose along-track position updates at a much lower rate than its ping rate (real case: a Klein SDF survey whose GPS fixes only every ~8 pings, jumping ~2m each time) has real gaps between along-track fixes wider than a resolution chosen from the average distance/ping can bridge at the default radius — the result grid shows periodic empty stripes at exactly the fix-to-fix interval, since most cells' nearest real point sits outside 1.5 * resolution_m. Passing a wider radius (e.g. the real fix-to-fix jump distance) bridges those gaps without also needing a coarser (more zoomed-out) resolution_m. Ignored if either of the two params below is given.

None along_search_radius_m float

Independent along-track / across-track search radii — an ellipse instead of a circle, in real (along_m, across_m) space. Each axis is rescaled by its own radius before the cKDTree is built/queried (then queried with a unit ball), which is exactly equivalent to an elliptical search with no custom distance metric needed. Default (None) for either falls back to search_radius_m (or its own default) — fully backward compatible with every existing caller.

Real motivation (2026-09-28): a swath's along-track (ping spacing) and across-track (sample interval) native resolutions can differ by an order of magnitude or more. The single isotropic search_radius_m this function used to have had to be wide enough to bridge real along-track gaps — which meant every cell's average also pooled far more across-track real detail than the data's own resolution supports, regardless of how fine resolution_m was set. A caller requesting a finer resolution_m for more real detail got more pixels of an equally over-smoothed image, not more detail — confirmed directly on real data as the cause of a "chips are blurry" report. Passing a narrow across_search_radius_m (sized to the real sample interval) alongside a wide along_search_radius_m (still sized to bridge real ping gaps) fixes this: real across-track texture is preserved instead of averaged away, without reintroducing along-track gaps.

None across_search_radius_m float

Independent along-track / across-track search radii — an ellipse instead of a circle, in real (along_m, across_m) space. Each axis is rescaled by its own radius before the cKDTree is built/queried (then queried with a unit ball), which is exactly equivalent to an elliptical search with no custom distance metric needed. Default (None) for either falls back to search_radius_m (or its own default) — fully backward compatible with every existing caller.

Real motivation (2026-09-28): a swath's along-track (ping spacing) and across-track (sample interval) native resolutions can differ by an order of magnitude or more. The single isotropic search_radius_m this function used to have had to be wide enough to bridge real along-track gaps — which meant every cell's average also pooled far more across-track real detail than the data's own resolution supports, regardless of how fine resolution_m was set. A caller requesting a finer resolution_m for more real detail got more pixels of an equally over-smoothed image, not more detail — confirmed directly on real data as the cause of a "chips are blurry" report. Passing a narrow across_search_radius_m (sized to the real sample interval) alongside a wide along_search_radius_m (still sized to bridge real ping gaps) fixes this: real across-track texture is preserved instead of averaged away, without reintroducing along-track gaps.

None avoid_edge_gaps bool

When True and the requested center is close enough to the edge of this channel's own recorded extent that the window would otherwise include genuine no-data cells (e.g. a target near the max-range edge of the swath), shift the center inward just enough to keep the full window inside real data instead -- same tradeoff extract_chip already makes for raw-pixel windows near an array edge. The target itself is then no longer necessarily at the window's exact center; locate_point against the original requested point still reports its true (now off-center) position correctly. Default False keeps the window exactly centered on the requested point regardless (this function's original, unconditional behavior) -- opt in per caller, since not every use of this function is a target-crop where "no data" is worse than "off-center".

False along_resolution_m float

Independent along-track / across-track meters-per-pixel — real, non-square output pixels. Default (None) for either falls back to resolution_m — fully backward compatible, every existing caller gets exactly the prior square-pixel behavior.

Real motivation (2026-09-29): even with anisotropic search radii (along_search_radius_m/across_search_radius_m above), a single shared resolution_m still forces the SAME pixel density on both axes. On a survey whose along-track native resolution is much coarser than across-track (ping spacing an order of magnitude or more wider than sample interval — one real survey measured at ~16:1), the along-track search radius floor (tied to real ping-to-ping gaps, independent of resolution_m — see along_search_radius_m above) ends up wide relative to a fine shared pixel spacing, visible in the output as elliptical averaging footprints — confirmed directly, real user report ("you can clearly see the ellipses which appear wide... that is not an issue w/ the radiometric"). No amount of tuning a single shared resolution_m/search radius eliminates this, because a plain pixel-space resize (which is what "radiometric" looks like) never averages a real neighborhood at all, so it has no footprint to show — it isn't solving the same problem. Setting along_resolution_m coarser than across_resolution_m (close to the real ping spacing) lets each axis's pixel size match its OWN real resolving power, eliminating the visible-footprint artifact without averaging away real across-track detail that IS there to resolve.

None across_resolution_m float

Independent along-track / across-track meters-per-pixel — real, non-square output pixels. Default (None) for either falls back to resolution_m — fully backward compatible, every existing caller gets exactly the prior square-pixel behavior.

Real motivation (2026-09-29): even with anisotropic search radii (along_search_radius_m/across_search_radius_m above), a single shared resolution_m still forces the SAME pixel density on both axes. On a survey whose along-track native resolution is much coarser than across-track (ping spacing an order of magnitude or more wider than sample interval — one real survey measured at ~16:1), the along-track search radius floor (tied to real ping-to-ping gaps, independent of resolution_m — see along_search_radius_m above) ends up wide relative to a fine shared pixel spacing, visible in the output as elliptical averaging footprints — confirmed directly, real user report ("you can clearly see the ellipses which appear wide... that is not an issue w/ the radiometric"). No amount of tuning a single shared resolution_m/search radius eliminates this, because a plain pixel-space resize (which is what "radiometric" looks like) never averages a real neighborhood at all, so it has no footprint to show — it isn't solving the same problem. Setting along_resolution_m coarser than across_resolution_m (close to the real ping spacing) lets each axis's pixel size match its OWN real resolving power, eliminating the visible-footprint artifact without averaging away real across-track detail that IS there to resolve.

None along_size_px int

Independent output row / column counts. Default (None) for either falls back to size_px. Combined with along_resolution_m/across_resolution_m, this is what actually makes the output array non-square in shape, not just in real-world meters-per-pixel — e.g. along_size_px=20 at along_resolution_m=0.4 covers the same real 8m as across_size_px=320 at across_resolution_m=0.025, and the returned array is genuinely (20, 320), not square. A caller displaying this gets correct proportions for free from most plotting libraries' default aspect handling (e.g. matplotlib imshow's aspect="equal", driven by array shape alone, with no extent needed) — it is not a stretched square image, it is a genuinely shorter/narrower real array.

None across_size_px int

Independent output row / column counts. Default (None) for either falls back to size_px. Combined with along_resolution_m/across_resolution_m, this is what actually makes the output array non-square in shape, not just in real-world meters-per-pixel — e.g. along_size_px=20 at along_resolution_m=0.4 covers the same real 8m as across_size_px=320 at across_resolution_m=0.025, and the returned array is genuinely (20, 320), not square. A caller displaying this gets correct proportions for free from most plotting libraries' default aspect handling (e.g. matplotlib imshow's aspect="equal", driven by array shape alone, with no extent needed) — it is not a stretched square image, it is a genuinely shorter/narrower real array.

None

Returns:

Type Description (grid, meta)

grid : (along_size_px, across_size_px) array (both default to size_px, reproducing the prior square shape unless overridden). NaN where no sample fell within the search radius of a cell. meta : dict with center_row/center_col (the requested center's own pixel position in grid — always the exact middle, since the grid is built centered on it by construction), the resolved along_min/across_min bounds, along_resolution_m/across_resolution_m (the resolved per-axis values, always present even when isotropic), and resolution_m — a legacy key kept for backward compatibility, equal to along_resolution_m; new code should read the per-axis keys instead, since this key is ambiguous once the two differ.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If no finite across_track_m/backscatter samples exist in channel_ds at all (e.g. entirely water column).

docs.title: extract_geometric_window_binned
docs.text:
extract_geometric_window_binned(
    channel_ds: Dataset,
    size_px: int,
    *,
    resolution_m: float,
    center_along_m: float,
    center_across_m: float,
    channel_idx: int | None = 0,
    backscatter_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    avoid_edge_gaps: bool = False,
    along_resolution_m: float | None = None,
    across_resolution_m: float | None = None,
    along_size_px: int | None = None,
    across_size_px: int | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, dict]

Same contract as :func:extract_geometric_window (same params, same (grid, meta) shape, same meta keys, drop-in interchangeable with :func:locate_point) but resamples via scipy.stats.binned_statistic_2d instead of a hand-written cKDTree.query_ball_point loop over every output cell.

2026-09-29, real user request, following this file's own established-libraries-first convention (see sidescanpy/CLAUDE.md's "Dependencies" section): once per-axis pixel resolution existed (along_resolution_m/across_resolution_m above), each output cell is really just "the mean of every real sample whose (along, across) position falls inside this cell's rectangle" — an ordinary 2D histogram-style binning, not a radius search. scipy already ships exactly that as a single vectorized call, so a custom per-cell loop wasn't buying anything.

Not a superset of the KDTree version — a genuinely different resampling philosophy, not just a faster implementation of the same one:

  • No search_radius_m/along_search_radius_m/ across_search_radius_m — a point either falls inside a cell's exact rectangle or it doesn't, there is no overlap/gap-bridging radius to tune. A cell with zero real samples inside its own rectangle is NaN, even if a real sample sits just across the boundary in the neighboring cell. This means a coarse along_resolution_m chosen to bridge real ping-to-ping gaps (the KDTree version's along_search_radius_m role) still works here — a wide-enough bin naturally contains the next ping's point — but an along_resolution_m finer than the real ping-to-ping spacing will show real empty cells between pings instead of the KDTree version's radius-bridged fill.
  • Strictly faster on real data (one vectorized scipy call instead of one Python-level query_ball_point call per output pixel), but not chosen for speed — chosen because "one real neighborhood per pixel, no radius tuning" is a more direct match for what along_resolution_m/across_resolution_m were already designed to express once they exist per-axis. See export/geometric_window.py's module tests (TestExtractGeometricWindowBinned) for a real-data comparison against the KDTree version at matching resolution.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If no finite across_track_m/backscatter samples exist in channel_ds at all (e.g. entirely water column).

docs.title: extract_geometric_window_griddata
docs.text:
extract_geometric_window_griddata(
    channel_ds: Dataset,
    size_px: int,
    *,
    resolution_m: float,
    center_along_m: float,
    center_across_m: float,
    channel_idx: int | None = 0,
    backscatter_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
    avoid_edge_gaps: bool = False,
    along_resolution_m: float | None = None,
    across_resolution_m: float | None = None,
    along_size_px: int | None = None,
    across_size_px: int | None = None,
    interp_method: str = "linear",
    max_fill_distance_m: float | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, dict]

Same contract as :func:extract_geometric_window/ :func:extract_geometric_window_binned (same params, same (grid, meta) shape, same meta keys, drop-in interchangeable with :func:locate_point) but resamples via scipy.interpolate.griddata -- full scattered-data interpolation across the whole requested grid, not a radius search (KDTree) or strict rectangle membership (binned).

2026-09-29, real user request/direction: an established-library resampling option with no NaN gaps by construction -- unlike :func:extract_geometric_window_binned, every output cell gets a value regardless of how sparse the real along-track sampling is relative to resolution_m, because griddata interpolates (and, for the small edge fraction outside the real data's convex hull, nearest-neighbor-extrapolates -- see below) rather than reporting "no real sample here."

This is a genuinely different tradeoff than the other two functions, not a strict improvement — say so plainly: at a resolution much finer than the real along-track sampling, the large majority of a griddata window's pixels are constructed by interpolation, not measured by the sensor. Real-data check (two real targets, resolution_m=0.03m, ~60-66% of cells with no real sample at that resolution): griddata never shows a gap, but most of what fills those gaps is triangulated from real points several real ping-widths away, not a resolved local measurement. Compare :func:extract_geometric_window (zero fabrication, real radius averaging) and :func:extract_geometric_window_binned (zero fabrication, real gaps shown honestly).

interp_method : "linear" (default), "cubic", or "nearest" -- passed straight through to scipy.interpolate. griddata's own method. "linear"/"cubic" leave NaN outside the real data's convex hull (no point to triangulate against there); those cells are automatically filled with a second, method="nearest" pass so this function never returns a gap regardless of interp_method -- "nearest" itself is already gap-free after the first pass. max_fill_distance_m : cells farther than this from every real sample are NaN -- outside the recorded swath (past max range, the nadir gap, the excluded channel of a single-channel window), where either pass above would otherwise extend the nearest edge sample into smeared wedges/streaks of invented seafloor (seen on chips wider than the swath). None (default) derives it from the data: 1.5x the larger of the 95th-percentile along-track ping gap, the median across-track sample step, and the output resolution -- so gaps between real pings/samples still interpolate. np.inf restores the old never-NaN behavior.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If no finite across_track_m/backscatter samples exist in channel_ds at all (e.g. entirely water column).

Georeferenced (northing x easting meters) windowed export.

Resamples a bounded square region directly at an explicit (resolution_m, size_px), centered on a given real-world lat/lon — builds on the survey-wide georeferencing/gridding path already in sidescanpy.grids. extract_georef_window(

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.image
docs.text:
Invertible 8-bit display transform.

Percentile-stretch + gamma-correct a backscatter array (any dtype) into an 8-bit grayscale image suitable for training-dataset export, while retaining enough metadata to reconstruct the original array later (lossy — 8-bit quantization is not exactly reversible, but the scale is recoverable). This is a display/export transform, not a physical correction — it has no relationship to processing/radiometric.py's TVG correction. Run TVG (and geometric/georef, if wanted) first; this module only turns whatever array it's handed into 8-bit.

Normalization scope (per-image vs. survey-wide vs. dataset-wide) is deliberately a caller decision, not baked in here: pass reference_stats=None (default) for per-image scope, where each array is stretched against its own percentiles, or precompute one :class:ReferenceStats via :func:compute_reference_stats over every window a wider scope should share and pass it to every :func:to_uint8 call in that scope.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: NORMALIZATION_SCOPES module-attribute
docs.text:
NORMALIZATION_SCOPES = ('image', 'shared')

"image": each image stretched on its own percentiles; "shared": one stretch for a whole set.

docs.title: ReversalMetadata dataclass
docs.text: Enough to invert :func:to_uint8 back to the original array's dtype and approximate scale.

docs.title: ReferenceStats dataclass
docs.text: Percentile bounds computed once, for reuse across many :func:to_uint8 calls at survey- or dataset-wide normalization scope, instead of each image normalizing against only its own window.

docs.title: compute_reference_stats
docs.text:
compute_reference_stats(
    *arrays: ndarray,
    pct_low: float = _DEFAULT_PCT_LOW,
    pct_high: float = _DEFAULT_PCT_HIGH,
) -> ReferenceStats

Compute shared percentile bounds over one or more arrays.

Call once over every window a survey-wide or dataset-wide normalization scope should share, then pass the result to every :func:to_uint8 call in that scope via reference_stats=. Omit entirely for the default per-image scope.

Non-finite values are excluded before the percentile is computed. Mixing arrays of different kinds (e.g. raw counts and TVG-corrected dB) is the caller's decision, not validated here — only combine arrays it actually makes sense to normalize together.

docs.title: to_uint8
docs.text:
to_uint8(
    array: ndarray,
    *,
    gamma: float = 1.0,
    pct_low: float = _DEFAULT_PCT_LOW,
    pct_high: float = _DEFAULT_PCT_HIGH,
    reference_stats: ReferenceStats | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, ReversalMetadata]

Percentile-stretch + gamma-correct array into an 8-bit grayscale image.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default array ndarray

uint16, uint32, or float32/float64. uint32 is stretched over non-zero values only (zero treated as background/no-return, matching raw sensor-counts convention); the other two kinds are stretched over all finite values.

required gamma float

Power-law display contrast (normalized ** gamma) — matches this library's existing display-gamma convention (viz.waterfall.plot_waterfall/viz.gridded, both of which hand gamma straight to matplotlib.colors.PowerNorm, whose own convention is normalized ** gamma), where 1.0 is a no-op. Since gamma > 1 on normalized in [0, 1] pushes values down (darkens midtones/background, compresses toward black), a caller reusing a gamma value tuned against a PowerNorm-based render (e.g. 2.5) gets the same visual direction here — the inverse convention (normalized ** (1/gamma), which brightens instead) was this function's original, undocumented-as-different implementation and produced washed-out/over-bright output at the same nominal gamma values that darkened contrast correctly elsewhere in this library; see CHANGELOG.md.

1.0 pct_low float

Percentile bounds for the stretch, matching this library's existing default elsewhere. Ignored when reference_stats is given.

(1.0, 99.0) pct_high float

Percentile bounds for the stretch, matching this library's existing default elsewhere. Ignored when reference_stats is given.

(1.0, 99.0) reference_stats ReferenceStats

Precomputed bounds (survey-/dataset-wide normalization scope, see :func:compute_reference_stats). When given, pct_low/ pct_high are ignored — the array is stretched against reference_stats's bounds instead of its own. Omit for the default per-image scope.

None

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.orientation
docs.text:
Display orientation for exported windows, and a display-only range detrend.

Every exported image is oriented to one display convention: pings run bottom-to-top (the newest ping at the top, matching EdgeTech Discover's target thumbnails), and a single port channel is mirrored so near range sits next to nadir on the same side as the starboard view's mirror image. Each function moves the annotated target positions (Target.sample = column, extra_attributes["window_row"] = row) together with the pixels.

  • :func:orient_for_display -- one decoded target window, one target.
  • :func:orient_pixel_window -- a sample/ping-space export window with any number of co-located targets.
  • :func:flip_geo_vertical / :func:orient_geo_window -- a resampled geometric (along/across meters) window.
  • :func:detrend_by_range -- display-only per-column median subtraction.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: detrend_by_range
docs.text:
detrend_by_range(window: ndarray) -> np.ndarray

Subtract each column's median across all pings (display only).

A flat-field-style correction: removes the typical level at each range so only deviations from it (targets, local texture) remain visible. It hides a left-to-right brightness gradient, such as a residual left by an imperfect TVG model, without correcting it -- not physically grounded and not a substitute for radiometric correction.

(n_pings, n_samples) array, sample axis last.

required

Same shape, centered near 0 rather than in the input units; render with percentile-based limits, not a fixed absolute scale.

docs.text:
orient_for_display(
    window: ndarray, target: Target
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, Target]

Orient a decoded target window to the export display convention.

Both flips match EdgeTech Discover's own target images (established by visual comparison, not from vendor documentation):

  • Vertical (always): decoded rows run in ascending ping order; the ping axis is reversed so the newest ping is at the top.
  • Horizontal (port only): a port window (target.channel == 0) is mirrored along the sample axis, matching the waterfall sign convention (port negative, starboard positive).

(n_pings, n_samples) decoded window, sample axis last.

required target Target

.channel controls the horizontal flip (anything but 0 skips it). extra_attributes["window_row"] is remapped if present.

required

Oriented window, and a copy of target with .sample and extra_attributes["window_row"] remapped to match.

  • Horizontal (single port channel only): channel_idx == 0 and style != "dual-swath" mirrors the sample axis. A dual-swath window is already port-mirrored by :func:~sidescanpy.export.windows.combine_channels_mirrored.

Targets use integer pixel-center coordinates, so a flip maps x -> n - 1 - x.

Always applies :func:flip_geo_vertical. A single port channel's window (combine=False, channel_idx == 0) is also mirrored horizontally: columns are built in ascending across_track_m, which is negative on port, so unmirrored port windows put near range on the right while starboard windows put it on the left. A combined (dual-swath) window spans both signs and already has nadir in the middle, so it is never mirrored.

The horizontal flip uses n - 1 - x on the target column, matching the long-standing export output.

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.ml.coco
docs.text:
COCO-format export for sonar targets.

Scoped to JSF for now: one canonical crop image + one bounding-box annotation per target, single category (no real class labels are assumed — Description/Tag are commonly empty), defaulting to min_confidence="verified" so a dataset export can't silently ship unlocalized or low-confidence boxes.

The bbox itself is a fixed placeholder size (box_size), not a measured target dimension — no source catalog seen so far has real LengthMeters/WidthMeters data. This is recorded in the written JSON's own info.description so the caveat travels with the file, not just with whatever presentation wraps it.

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: CocoImageEntry dataclass
docs.text:
One target's canonical crop, ready to become a COCO image+annotation.

Multiple entries may share the same file_name — e.g. every cataloged target that falls within one exported window (see sidescanpy.export.windows.targets_within_window). They become one shared COCO image record with one annotation per entry, rather than one image per target. Every entry sharing a file_name must agree on width/height (the same physical image).

bbox_size, if given, overrides write_coco/write_yolo's global box_size for this entry only — for a real, measured target extent instead of the shared placeholder.

target=None records an image with no annotations (a background image): COCO gets the image record alone, YOLO an empty label file. Such entries bypass the confidence filter.

write_coco(
    entries: list[CocoImageEntry],
    output_path: str | Path,
    *,
    category_name: str = "target",
    box_size: tuple[float, float] = (40.0, 40.0),
    min_confidence: str = "verified",
    categories: list[str] | None = None,
) -> dict

Write entries to output_path as a COCO-format JSON dataset.

Per-annotation class comes from Target.category (None -> category_name). The categories list is the sorted set of names present with ids 1..N, or, if categories is given, that explicit ordered list (see :func:resolve_categories). With no categorized targets the output is the single category_name category, id 1.

Only targets with position_confidence at or above min_confidence (ordered unknown < approximate < verified) are included — pass min_confidence="approximate" or "unknown" explicitly to include lower-confidence targets; this must be an opt-in, not the default, per the design doc's own rationale (a prior export in a sibling project shipped an unverified/wrong bounding-box hypothesis by not gating on this).

Entries sharing a file_name become one image with multiple annotations (see CocoImageEntry's own docstring) — each entry's own bbox_size (if set) is used for its box, else the shared box_size. An entry with target=None adds its image with no annotation.

Returns the dict that was written, for inline inspection/testing.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If two entries share a file_name but disagree on width/height.

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.ml.dataset
docs.text:
Annotated training datasets of target-centered (and background) images.

:func:build_target_dataset turns converted .ss.h5 surveys plus a target catalog into one COCO + YOLO dataset per export style, rendered at one render level and configured by a :class:DatasetSpec:

  1. Targets at or above min_confidence are correlated to their ping (:func:~sidescanpy.targets.correlate.correlate_target) and grouped by file and frequency.
  2. For each target a bounded ping neighborhood is loaded once and every style is cut from it n_augment times (independent jitter, optional random flip). Every catalog target inside a window becomes an annotation.
  3. Optionally, n_background screened no-target windows per style (:func:~sidescanpy.export.windows.sample_background_windows).
  4. Images are written as single-channel 8- or 16-bit PNGs, with targets.coco.json, a YOLO label set, augmentations.json (when draws vary) and a top-level manifest.json.

Plotting (contact sheets, context views) is optional and supplied by the caller as callables, so this module never imports matplotlib.

Output layout per style directory (layout="flat", the default)::

<style>/target_<id>[_a<k>].png, bg_<n>[_a<k>].png
<style>/targets.coco.json
<style>/targets.yolo/{data.yaml,labels/<stem>.txt}
<style>/augmentations.json       (n_augment > 1, random_flip or backgrounds)
<style>/splits/{train,val}.txt   (val_fraction > 0)

layout="ultralytics"::

<style>/images/{train,val}/<file>.png
<style>/labels/{train,val}/<stem>.txt
<style>/{train,val}.coco.json
<style>/data.yaml                (Ultralytics dataset file)

With several resolutions each gets its own res_<m>m/ directory.

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.ml.yolo
docs.text:
YOLO-format export for sonar targets.

Mirrors export/ml/coco.py's write_coco — same input (CocoImageEntry list, despite the name it's just "one target's canonical crop", not COCO-specific), same min_confidence gating, same placeholder box_size caveat (no measured target dimension exists in any source catalog seen so far). Kept as a separate writer rather than a shared abstraction over both formats because the two output shapes (one JSON tree vs. one label file per image + a class list) don't share much beyond "filter, then compute a box".

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: write_yolo
docs.text:
write_yolo(
    entries: list[CocoImageEntry],
    output_dir: str | Path,
    *,
    category_name: str = "target",
    box_size: tuple[float, float] = (40.0, 40.0),
    min_confidence: str = "verified",
    categories: list[str] | None = None,
    labels_dir: str | Path | None = None,
    data_yaml: bool = True,
) -> dict

Write entries to output_dir as a YOLO-format label set.

Same inclusion filtering as write_coco (position_confidence at or above min_confidence, opt-in only for lower confidence), and the same multi-entries-per-file_name grouping (one label file gets one line per entry sharing that file_name, instead of the last one silently overwriting the rest) — see CocoImageEntry's own docstring. Writes one label file per image at output_dir/labels/<Path(file_name).stem>.txt — one class_id cx cy w h line per box, normalized to [0, 1] by that image's own width/height (the YOLO convention) — plus a output_dir/data.yaml naming the single class. Each entry's own bbox_size (if set) is used for its box, else the shared box_size. An entry with target=None contributes an image with an empty label file (a background image).

labels_dir overrides where label files go (default output_dir/labels); data_yaml=False skips data.yaml (for callers that write their own dataset file, e.g. per split).

Returns a dict of what was written ({"names": [...], "images": [...]}, one entry per included image with its label path), for inline inspection/testing — YOLO has no single canonical in-memory representation the way COCO's JSON dict does.

Class index is the position in the sorted set of Target.category names present (uncategorized -> category_name), or in the explicit ordered categories list if given; data.yaml lists the same order. See resolve_categories.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If two entries share a file_name but disagree on width/height.

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.windows
docs.text:
Export windows: where an image is cut from a survey, and what is in it.

  • :mod:~sidescanpy.export.windows.pixel -- sample/ping-space crops (chips, full-channel views), co-located targets, and the per-style window for the uncorrected/db/radiometric render levels.
  • :mod:~sidescanpy.export.windows.levels -- styles, render levels and the backscatter variable each level reads.
  • :mod:~sidescanpy.export.windows.neighborhood -- bounded, block-averaged ping neighborhoods for the real-meters levels.
  • :mod:~sidescanpy.export.windows.geo -- geometric/georef windows.
  • :mod:~sidescanpy.export.windows.background -- screened no-target windows.
  • :mod:~sidescanpy.export.windows.native -- chips and dual-swath tiles that are square/scaled in metres on the native ping x sample grid, with pixel <-> native mapping (annotation round trips).

2026 rshomberg@uri.edu

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.windows.background
docs.text:
Background (no-target) export windows.

A detector trained only on target-centered images never sees an empty frame. :func:sample_background_windows samples window centers across a set of converted surveys, renders each one through the same window extractors as target windows (:func:~sidescanpy.export.windows.pixel.extract_pixel_style_window, :func:~sidescanpy.export.windows.geo.extract_geo_style_window), and keeps only windows that

  1. contain no cataloged target within the window plus margin_m. Every catalog target (any confidence) is correlated to its ping with :func:~sidescanpy.targets.correlate.correlate_target, projected onto every frequency of its file (:func:~sidescanpy.targets.correlate.place_catalog), and located in the rendered window with the same lookup target windows use for co-located targets. A conservative geographic guard additionally rejects a window whose reach from nadir (plus margin) covers any target's recorded lat/lon -- this catches targets on another file, another line crossing the same ground, or targets that never correlated;
  2. are mostly data: at most max_nan_frac of the rendered cells are NaN (outside coverage, nadir gap, cropped far range).

Background windows are only as clean as the target catalog: an object the catalog misses can appear in one and be learned as background.

Resolution (unless resolution_m_override): chip -- the native max(meters_per_sample, ping_spacing); swath styles -- the swath width over size_px, floored at the ping spacing. With swath_fill (swath styles, no override) the frame instead spans the across-track extent the data fills (:func:swath_fill_extent) at square pixels, with no ping-spacing floor and not pinned to nadir.

geometric windows include every co-located candidate from items_by_channel (both channels for dual swath) and are oriented with :func:~sidescanpy.export.orientation.orient_geo_window. georef windows carry only the primary target and are not reoriented (rows follow northing).

resample_method selects the geometric resampler: "kdtree" (average of measurements within a search radius; no fabricated values, some directional blur), "binned" (per-cell mean of the samples inside it; empty cells stay NaN) or "griddata" (scipy interpolation; no gaps inside coverage, but at a resolution finer than the ping spacing most cells are interpolated). georef always uses :func:~sidescanpy.export.georef_window.extract_georef_window.

docs.text:
Export styles, render levels, and the backscatter variables each level reads.

A style is the window shape (chip: a tight single-channel crop; single-swath: one full channel; dual-swath: both channels side by side). A render level is the processing state and coordinate system the window is rendered in: uncorrected/db/radiometric crop native sample/ping pixels; geometric/georef resample onto a real-meters grid.

Neither uncorrected nor backscatter_db is stored on disk: they are derived per loaded neighborhood by :func:with_uncorrected_var and :func:with_db_var.

docs.title: sidescanpy.export.windows.native
docs.text:
Native slant-range windows that are square in metres.

Sidescan pings are often much further apart along track than samples are across track (e.g. 24 cm between pings, 2.4 cm between samples). Resampling such data onto a fine metric grid repeats or smears pings; cropping a square of native pixels squashes shapes by the same ratio. The windows here cut a region that is square (chip) or a fixed length (tile) in metres from the native ping x sample grid and resize it with linear interpolation, so the native detail is kept and shapes have their true proportions.

  • :func:native_chip -- one side, centred on a target, size_m square.
  • :func:swath_tiles -- the whole survey as consecutive dual-swath tiles (port mirrored on the left, starboard on the right), e.g. for annotating every object.
  • :class:NativeWindow -- where an image sits in native (ping, sample, channel) space, with conversions both ways, so boxes drawn on an image can be turned back into sonar coordinates and re-cut at another scale.

Ping and sample arguments are positions along the dataset's ping and sample axes. Values are taken from value_var as stored (dB after the tvg step); convert to an image with :func:sidescanpy.export.image.to_uint8.

docs.title: extract_chip
docs.text:
extract_chip(
    array: ndarray,
    center_row: float,
    center_col: float,
    size_px: int,
    *,
    jitter_px: int = 0,
    rng: Generator | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, WindowExtent]

Fixed size_px x size_px crop around (center_row, center_col).

Non-padding placement: the window shifts inward near an array edge instead of zero-padding, trading perfect centering for "always full real data." jitter_px (default 0, exact centering) randomizes which point the window centers on, so a detector doesn't learn "the target is always dead-center" — the true target position is unaffected, only where the window lands moves.

If array is smaller than size_px in a given axis, the full available extent on that axis is returned instead (non-square output) rather than padding — confirmed against real per-target survey data where a source catalog's own decoded window can have a hard ping-count ceiling well under a requested chip size. Every caller downstream (CocoImageEntry, write_coco/write_yolo) already carries per-image width/height explicitly, so a dataset with mixed image sizes from this cause is handled correctly, not silently mis-sized.

Returns:

Type Description (window, extent)

docs.title: extract_full_channel
docs.text:
extract_full_channel(
    array: ndarray,
    *,
    center_ping: float | None = None,
    square: bool = True,
    fixed_ping_count: int = 200,
    jitter_px: int = 0,
    rng: Generator | None = None,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, WindowExtent]

Full-sample-axis window spanning a fixed ping span, at native resolution — not resized here. Resize (via :func:resize_to) belongs after a photometric transform (e.g. :func:sidescanpy.export.image.to_uint8) has run on the full native-resolution values, not before it: computing a percentile stretch on an already-downsampled array measures the stretch against a blurred, artificially low-variance distribution and washes the result out (found the hard way — see this function's own history). Every other statistics-computing function in this library (waterfall/ gridded percentile scaling, resample_channel_to_grid's cell aggregation) works the same way: aggregate/stretch against real per-sample values first, resize the result for display second.

square=True (default): the native ping span equals the channel's own sample count, not a fixed ping count against a differing sample count — avoids the aspect-ratio stretch a fixed ping count would otherwise introduce once the eventual square output is produced. square=False uses fixed_ping_count pings instead.

center_ping defaults to the array's own midpoint (a full-channel negative sample has no target to center on); pass a target's ping position for a positive sample. jitter_px behaves as in :func:extract_chip.

Known, deliberately deferred edge case: a survey shorter than the native ping span raises ValueError rather than guessing a workaround (e.g. padding or falling back to non-square) — revisit if a real survey actually hits this.

Returns:

Type Description (window, extent)

Native resolution — pass through a photometric transform, then :func:resize_to, in that order.

docs.title: utm_crs_for_lonlat
docs.text:
utm_crs_for_lonlat(lon: float, lat: float) -> CRS

Pick the WGS84 UTM zone CRS containing (lon, lat).

Standard "auto-UTM" heuristic: zone = floor((lon + 180) / 6) + 1, hemisphere from the sign of lat. EPSG 326xx for northern- hemisphere zones, 327xx for southern. Good enough to pick a sane projected CRS automatically for a survey's gridded output; near a zone boundary (every 6° of longitude) the "correct" zone is a judgment call anyway — pass an explicit CRS via GridDefinition if a specific zone/datum is required (e.g. matching a state-plane system already in use for a project).

Parameters:

WGS84 degrees. Typically the center of the survey's bbox.

required lat float

required

docs.title: to_dataset
docs.text:
to_dataset() -> xr.Dataset

This raster as a plain xr.Dataset on 1-D cell-center axes.

Dims ("y", "x") with 1-D y/x coordinates (northing/ easting in metres for a projected CRS, latitude/longitude in degrees for a geographic one), in this raster's own row order (south to north). Every data variable of :attr:dataset (backscatter, plus n_contributing_samples when present) is carried over with its attrs, and the CRS is stored CF-style in a scalar spatial_ref coordinate (crs_wkt / spatial_ref attrs, referenced from each variable's grid_mapping), which rioxarray, GDAL and most CF readers recognize. Needs no optional dependency.

The grid's cell centers are evenly spaced but, because GridDefinition stretches ceil(extent / resolution_m) cells across the bbox, the spacing is only approximately resolution_m; x/y hold the real centers.

docs.title: sidescanpy.grids.resample
docs.text:
Resampling channel data to georeferenced grids.

Provides resample_channel_to_grid() to aggregate sidescan backscatter from survey geometry to a regular grid using various aggregation methods, and grid_channel() to do so on a UTM grid fit to the channel's own extent.

docs.title: ResamplingMethod
docs.text:
Bases: str, Enum

Resampling aggregation method.

docs.title: resample_channel_to_grid
docs.text:
resample_channel_to_grid(
    channel: Dataset,
    grid_def: GridDefinition,
    method: ResamplingMethod = ResamplingMethod.MEAN,
    separate_sides: bool = False,
    max_search_radius_m: Optional[float] = None,
    backscatter_var: str = "backscatter_intensity",
) -> SideScanGriddedRaster

Resample channel backscatter to a regular grid.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default channel Dataset

Channel dataset with a backscatter variable (see backscatter_var) and per-sample coordinates (latitude_per_sample, longitude_per_sample).

required grid_def GridDefinition

Target grid definition (bbox, resolution, CRS).

required method ResamplingMethod

Aggregation method: mean, median, max, nearest, or idw.

"mean" separate_sides bool

If True, output separate port and starboard bands (diagnostic mode). If False, merge port and starboard into single backscatter variable.

False max_search_radius_m float

Maximum search radius in meters. If None, use 1.5x grid resolution.

None backscatter_var str

Name of the backscatter variable in channel to resample. Corrections are applied in place to "backscatter_intensity" (dB once TVG has run, linear amplitude before); for the uncorrected signal of a corrected channel, assign sidescanpy.processing.uncorrected_backscatter(channel) to a variable and grid that.

"backscatter_intensity" Notes

This function does not filter out or otherwise special-case the TVG floor-clipped sample population (see apply_tvg()'s "KNOWN ISSUE" docstring note). Those samples generally have finite georeferenced coordinates, so they pass the np.isfinite(lat)/ np.isfinite(lon) filter here like any other sample and get included in each cell's aggregation. With method=MEAN (the default) and typical real-survey point densities (thousands of raw samples per cell at 1m resolution), that ~1% outlier population gets diluted, not removed — it's swamped by the majority-real samples in the same cell, not excluded from the average. This dilution is exactly why a gridded raster's effective dynamic range (and therefore its percentile-based color scale) can differ sharply from a per-sample waterfall's.

Returns:

Type Description SideScanGriddedRaster

Gridded backscatter raster with n_contributing_samples tracking.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If channel is missing required variables or grid bounds don't overlap.
